title: Azure Fundamentals
subtitle: 20 questions across cloud concepts, Azure services, identity, and governance

questions.q: A company runs virtual machines on Azure where they manage the OS, middleware, and applications themselves. Which cloud service model does this represent?
questions.note: IaaS gives you the virtual hardware — you manage everything above the hypervisor, including the OS, runtime, and applications. Azure Virtual Machines is the canonical Azure IaaS example.

explain.correct: Azure Virtual Machines is IaaS: Azure manages the physical hardware and hypervisor, and you are responsible for the OS, patches, middleware, and your application.
wrong: SaaS delivers a fully managed application to the end user (e.g., Microsoft 365). The customer manages nothing below the application layer.
PaaS provides a managed runtime and platform so developers can deploy code without managing the OS. Azure App Service is the Azure PaaS example.
FaaS (serverless) abstracts even the runtime away; Azure Functions charges only per execution and scales to zero — no VM management at all.

questions.q: A developer deploys a web application to Azure App Service without configuring or patching the underlying operating system. Which cloud model is Azure App Service?
questions.note: Azure App Service is a Platform as a Service (PaaS) offering. Microsoft manages the OS, runtime, and scaling infrastructure; the customer only manages the application code and data.

explain.correct: App Service is PaaS: the OS, runtime patches, and horizontal scaling are handled by Azure, leaving the developer to focus solely on application code.
wrong: IaaS requires the customer to manage the OS and middleware. App Service removes that responsibility entirely.
SaaS is a fully delivered end-user application like Microsoft 365 or Dynamics 365. App Service hosts applications you build, not a Microsoft-delivered end-user product.
On-premises means hardware and software owned and operated in a customer's own datacenter, with no Azure involvement.

questions.q: In the shared responsibility model, which TWO items remain ALWAYS the customer's responsibility regardless of the service model chosen (IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS)?
options: Physical datacenter security and network hardware
Operating system patching and runtime management
Data stored in the service and identity/account management
questions.note: Across all three cloud models, the customer always retains responsibility for their own data and for managing identities (accounts and access). Microsoft's shared responsibility documentation explicitly lists these as permanent customer duties.

explain.correct: Data classification and protection, and identity/access management, are always the customer's responsibility regardless of whether they chose IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
wrong: Physical datacenter and network hardware are always Microsoft's responsibility in any Azure service model — the customer never touches physical infrastructure.
OS patching responsibility shifts depending on model: customer-owned in IaaS, Microsoft-owned in PaaS and SaaS.
The hypervisor and host hardware are always managed by Microsoft across all Azure service models.

questions.q: An organization wants to eliminate large upfront server purchases and instead pay a predictable monthly fee for Azure resources. Which financial shift does this represent?
questions.note: Moving to the cloud converts capital expenditure (buying hardware) into operational expenditure (paying for consumption). This improves cash flow and shifts IT spend from the balance sheet to the income statement.

explain.correct: Cloud adoption converts CapEx (large upfront hardware purchases) to OpEx (ongoing operational subscription or consumption payments), freeing capital and improving financial agility.
wrong: OpEx to CapEx is the opposite direction — that would mean moving from a subscription model back to buying hardware outright, which is counter to cloud adoption.
Depreciation and amortization are accounting methods, not the business model shift described by cloud adoption.
Sunk cost refers to money already spent that cannot be recovered; it is an accounting concept unrelated to the CapEx-to-OpEx cloud migration rationale.

questions.q: What is an Azure Availability Zone?
options: A geographic area containing multiple Azure regions
A physically separate datacenter within a single Azure region, with independent power, cooling, and networking
A paired secondary region used for disaster recovery
A logical container that groups related Azure resources
questions.note: An Availability Zone is one or more physically distinct datacenters within a single region. Each zone has its own power, cooling, and networking. A minimum of three zones exist in each AZ-enabled region, protecting against single-datacenter failure.

explain.correct: An Availability Zone is a physically separate datacenter within one Azure region. Deploying across multiple zones protects against datacenter-level failures, not region-level failures.
wrong: A geography (geo) is the large area grouping multiple regions (e.g., 'Europe'). An Availability Zone is far smaller — it sits inside a single region.
A region pair is two Azure regions far apart geographically, used for cross-region disaster recovery and sequential platform updates. It is a region-level, not datacenter-level, construct.
A logical container that groups resources is a Resource Group — a management construct, not an infrastructure unit.

questions.q: Why does Azure pair regions (region pairs)?
options: To provide low-latency connections between VNets inside one datacenter
To enable cross-region disaster recovery and ensure platform updates are applied to only one region at a time
To satisfy Availability Zone minimum requirements of three datacenters
To share the same physical hardware between two customer subscriptions
questions.note: Region pairs serve two primary purposes: geographic disaster recovery (replication to a partner region) and sequential platform maintenance (Azure updates one paired region before the other, limiting blast radius).

explain.correct: Region pairs are two Azure regions separated by at least 300 miles. They support cross-region DR data replication and ensure that planned maintenance only rolls out to one paired region at a time.
wrong: Low-latency VNet connections within one datacenter are handled by Availability Zones and VNet peering, not region pairs.
Availability Zones require a minimum of three physically separate datacenters within one region. Region pairs operate at an entirely different geographic scale.
Region pairs are infrastructure-level constructs for resilience and maintenance sequencing — they have nothing to do with sharing hardware between subscriptions.

questions.q: A company needs a managed Kubernetes orchestration service on Azure so their container teams do not have to manage the control plane. Which Azure service should they use?
questions.note: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is a managed Kubernetes offering where Azure manages the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler) for free; customers manage and pay for worker nodes.

explain.correct: AKS is the managed Kubernetes service — Azure provisions, upgrades, and monitors the Kubernetes control plane so teams can focus on deploying workloads, not managing cluster infrastructure.
wrong: Azure Container Instances runs individual containers on demand without orchestration. It is not a Kubernetes cluster — there is no scheduler, node pool management, or pod orchestration.
Azure App Service is a PaaS web hosting platform for applications and APIs, not a container orchestration system.
Azure Batch is a job scheduling service for large-scale parallel and HPC workloads, not container orchestration.

questions.q: A developer wants to run backend code triggered by an HTTP request and pay only for the milliseconds the code executes, with no server to manage. Which Azure compute option is the best fit?
questions.note: Azure Functions is Azure's serverless compute offering. Code runs in response to events or HTTP triggers and billing is per-execution and per GB-second of memory consumed. There is no always-on infrastructure to manage.

explain.correct: Azure Functions is serverless: no VMs to manage, no idle costs, and billing is purely consumption-based (per execution + per GB-second). It scales automatically from zero.
wrong: Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS — you pay for the VM whether or not code is running, and you manage the OS, patches, and runtime.
An App Service Plan (Standard tier) is an always-on managed platform. It runs 24/7 and you pay for the plan tier regardless of traffic volume.
Azure Dedicated Host provisions an entire physical server exclusively for your organization — the opposite of serverless, and far more costly and complex than needed here.

questions.q: A company needs a dedicated PRIVATE network connection between their on-premises datacenter and Azure that does NOT travel over the public internet. Which Azure service provides this?
questions.note: Azure ExpressRoute establishes a private, dedicated circuit between on-premises infrastructure and Azure through a connectivity provider. Traffic never crosses the public internet, offering higher reliability, lower latency, and consistent bandwidth.

explain.correct: ExpressRoute uses a private circuit via a connectivity provider — traffic is isolated from the public internet, delivering predictable performance and higher security than a VPN tunnel.
wrong: Azure VPN Gateway Site-to-Site creates an encrypted IPsec tunnel, but the tunnel travels OVER the public internet. It does not provide a private dedicated circuit.
Azure Virtual Network (VNet) is an isolated private network within Azure itself. It does not create a physical or logical connection to on-premises infrastructure.
Azure Front Door is a global application delivery and CDN service for HTTP/HTTPS traffic acceleration — it has no role in private datacenter-to-Azure connectivity.

questions.q: What does an Azure Network Security Group (NSG) do?
options: Provides a dedicated private connection from on-premises to Azure
Acts as a stateful firewall filtering inbound and outbound traffic for subnets or NICs
Assigns public IP addresses to virtual machines
Routes traffic between Azure regions using Microsoft's backbone
questions.note: An NSG contains security rules with allow/deny decisions for inbound and outbound traffic. It is stateful — if an inbound connection is permitted, the return traffic is automatically allowed. NSGs attach to subnets or individual network interfaces.

explain.correct: An NSG is a stateful Layer 4 firewall. Rules specify protocol, port, and source/destination. Because it is stateful, allowed connection return traffic flows automatically without a matching outbound rule.
wrong: A dedicated private on-premises connection is Azure ExpressRoute, not an NSG.
Public IP addresses are a separate Azure resource assigned to a VM's NIC or load balancer. NSGs filter traffic; they do not assign addressing.
Routing traffic across regions over Microsoft's backbone is performed by Azure Virtual WAN or Global VNet Peering — not NSGs, which are local traffic filters.

questions.q: Which Azure Blob Storage access tier is CHEAPEST for storage cost per GB but requires several hours to retrieve data and incurs a high retrieval fee?
questions.note: The Archive tier costs the least per GB stored but data is offline and can take up to 15 hours to rehydrate. It is designed for data that is rarely or never accessed, such as compliance backups and long-term audit logs.

explain.correct: Archive is the cheapest storage tier per GB. However, data must be 'rehydrated' (moved to Hot or Cool) before it can be read, which can take up to 15 hours and incurs a per-GB retrieval fee.
wrong: Hot tier has the highest storage cost per GB but the lowest access/retrieval cost. It is designed for frequently accessed data.
Cool tier has lower storage costs than Hot but higher retrieval costs. Data remains online and is accessible immediately — unlike Archive.
Cold tier (added after Cool) offers lower storage costs than Cool but still provides online data access without the hours-long rehydration that Archive requires.

questions.q: A company needs their Azure Storage data replicated across multiple datacenters WITHIN the same Azure region to protect against a single-datacenter failure, but they do NOT need cross-region protection. Which redundancy option should they choose?
questions.note: ZRS replicates data synchronously across three Availability Zones within a single region. This protects against datacenter (zone) failure. LRS keeps all three copies in a single datacenter. GRS and GZRS replicate to a paired region for cross-region protection.

explain.correct: ZRS synchronously writes three copies across three Availability Zones in one region. If one zone (datacenter) fails, data remains available from the other two zones — with no cross-region replication.
wrong: LRS replicates data three times within a SINGLE datacenter. If that datacenter fails, all copies are lost simultaneously. It does not protect against datacenter failure.
GRS replicates data to a paired region (cross-region DR), which is more protection than required here and adds cost. It does not distribute copies across zones in the primary region.
GZRS combines ZRS in the primary region WITH geo-replication to a secondary paired region — more protection than required here and at higher cost.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes what an Azure Storage account holds?
options: Only relational database tables for Azure SQL Database
A container for Blob, Files, Queue, and Table storage services under a single namespace and billing unit
Exclusively file shares for Azure NetApp Files
A compute quota allocation for a subscription
questions.note: An Azure Storage account provides a unique namespace and serves as the billing and security boundary for Blob Storage, Azure Files (SMB/NFS file shares), Queue Storage, and Table Storage. All four services live under one account.

explain.correct: A storage account is the top-level container for all four core Azure Storage services: Blob (unstructured objects), Files (managed file shares), Queue (message queues), and Table (NoSQL key-value).
wrong: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed relational database service and has its own separate resource type. It is not hosted inside a storage account.
Azure NetApp Files is a separate enterprise-grade NFS/SMB service built on NetApp technology. It has its own resource type and does not use Azure Storage accounts.
Compute quotas are subscription-level limits managed by the Azure Resource Manager, not by storage accounts.

questions.q: Which Azure database service is a fully managed, globally distributed NoSQL database designed for low-latency access at planet scale?
questions.note: Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's multi-model, globally distributed NoSQL database. It guarantees single-digit millisecond latency at the 99th percentile, supports multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table), and can replicate data to any Azure region.

explain.correct: Cosmos DB is a globally distributed NoSQL database with multi-region write support, multiple API models, and sub-10ms read/write latency SLAs. It is purpose-built for planet-scale applications.
wrong: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed relational (SQL) database engine based on Microsoft SQL Server. It supports T-SQL and relational schemas — it is not NoSQL.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL is a managed open-source relational database service. Like SQL Database, it is relational, not a globally distributed NoSQL engine.
Azure Synapse Analytics is a data warehousing and big-data analytics service. It is designed for analytical workloads (OLAP), not low-latency transactional NoSQL access.

questions.q: What is Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory)?
options: An on-premises domain controller service equivalent to Windows Server Active Directory
Azure's cloud-based identity and access management service for authenticating users and applications
A network firewall that filters traffic based on user identity
A database for storing customer relationship data
questions.note: Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity platform used to authenticate users to Azure, Microsoft 365, and thousands of SaaS applications. It is NOT a cloud version of Windows Server AD — it uses modern protocols (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, SAML) and has no domain controller concept.

explain.correct: Microsoft Entra ID is Azure's cloud identity service. It handles authentication and authorization for Azure resources, Microsoft 365, and integrated third-party SaaS apps using modern identity protocols.
wrong: Windows Server Active Directory is an on-premises directory service using LDAP and Kerberos, with domain controllers and group policy. Entra ID is a cloud service with entirely different architecture and protocols — it is not a cloud lift-and-shift of on-prem AD.
A network firewall filters traffic at the network layer. While Conditional Access in Entra ID can factor in network location, Entra ID itself is an identity service, not a firewall.
CRM data storage is the domain of Dynamics 365 or third-party CRM platforms. Microsoft Entra ID stores identity objects (users, groups, apps), not customer business records.

questions.q: Which Azure RBAC role allows a user to manage ALL Azure resources in a scope (create, update, delete) but NOT grant access to others?
questions.note: Contributor can create, update, and delete Azure resources but cannot assign roles to other users. Owner has all Contributor permissions PLUS the ability to grant access. Reader is read-only. User Access Administrator can only manage access, not resources.

explain.correct: Contributor grants full create/read/update/delete rights over Azure resources at the assigned scope, but it explicitly excludes role assignment. Only Owner and User Access Administrator can grant access.
wrong: Owner has ALL permissions including role assignment. The question specifically excludes the ability to grant access to others, which rules out Owner.
Reader is read-only — it cannot create, update, or delete any resources.
User Access Administrator can manage role assignments but cannot create or manage Azure resources. It is the inverse of the capability described.

questions.q: An organization structures its Azure environment with four tiers: a root container for applying policies across all subscriptions, individual billing and resource deployment units, logical groupings of related resources, and individual deployable items. Which option correctly names these four tiers from highest to lowest?
options: Subscription → Management Group → Resource Group → Resource
Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource
Resource Group → Subscription → Management Group → Resource
questions.note: The Azure resource hierarchy is: Management Group (top) → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource. Policies and RBAC applied at a higher level inherit downward. Every resource belongs to exactly one resource group, and every resource group belongs to exactly one subscription.

explain.correct: Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource is the correct Azure governance hierarchy. Governance (policy, RBAC) flows downward: settings at the Management Group level apply to all subscriptions and resources beneath it.
wrong: Subscription → Management Group is reversed. Management Groups sit ABOVE subscriptions and apply governance to them, not the other way around.
Resource Group → Subscription → Management Group is completely reversed — resources are at the bottom of the hierarchy, not near the top.
Tenant is the Microsoft Entra ID organization boundary, not an Azure resource management tier. Region is an infrastructure concept, not a resource hierarchy level.

questions.q: What happens to all resources inside an Azure Resource Group when the Resource Group itself is deleted?
options: Resources are moved to the default Resource Group in the same subscription
All resources inside the Resource Group are permanently deleted (cascade delete)
The deletion is blocked until each resource is individually removed first
Resources are archived to Azure Blob Storage for 30 days
questions.note: Deleting an Azure Resource Group is a cascading operation — every resource contained within it is deleted simultaneously. This is by design and is why Resource Groups are the unit of lifecycle management: development environments, for example, can be torn down with a single delete.

explain.correct: Resource Group deletion cascades: all child resources are permanently deleted in one operation. This is a core design feature allowing lifecycle management at the group level.
wrong: There is no automatic resource migration to a default Resource Group. Azure does not move resources when their Resource Group is deleted — they are destroyed.
Azure does not require individual resource deletion before removing a Resource Group. The cascade delete handles everything in one command.
Azure does not archive resources to Blob Storage on deletion. Once a Resource Group is deleted, the resources within it are gone — there is no 30-day recovery window through this mechanism.

questions.q: A security team wants to PREVENT anyone in the organization from creating Azure resources outside of approved regions, regardless of their RBAC role. Which governance tool enforces this?
questions.note: Azure Policy defines and enforces rules about WHAT can be created (e.g., allowed locations, allowed SKUs, required tags). RBAC controls WHO can perform actions. Policy can block non-compliant resource creation for everyone, including Owners.

explain.correct: Azure Policy enforces organizational standards on resource configuration — including allowed regions, allowed VM sizes, and required tags. A 'Deny' policy effect blocks non-compliant resources from being created regardless of the user's RBAC role.
wrong: RBAC controls WHO can create, read, update, or delete resources. It does not constrain WHAT configuration is allowed — a Contributor can deploy to any region unless Policy blocks them.
Azure Resource Locks (CanNotDelete / ReadOnly) protect existing resources from modification or deletion. They do not govern WHERE or HOW new resources are created.

Azure Blueprints is a repeatable governance package that can bundle policies and RBAC assignments together. However, the enforcement of the location rule itself comes from Azure Policy — Blueprints is the deployment vehicle, not the enforcement engine.

questions.q: A finance team wants to estimate the MONTHLY COST of a new Azure deployment BEFORE provisioning any resources. Which Azure tool should they use?
options: Azure TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) Calculator
questions.note: The Azure Pricing Calculator allows teams to configure specific services, regions, tiers, and quantities to estimate costs before deployment. Azure Cost Management shows actual spend on running resources. The TCO Calculator compares on-premises costs to Azure costs.

explain.correct: The Azure Pricing Calculator is the pre-deployment estimation tool. You select services, configure options (region, SKU, hours), and get a monthly cost estimate before spending a dollar.
wrong: Azure Cost Management + Billing analyzes and reports on ACTUAL, incurred spend on already-deployed resources. It cannot estimate future costs for resources that do not yet exist.
Azure Advisor provides personalized recommendations for cost optimization, security, reliability, and performance on EXISTING deployed resources. It is not a pre-deployment estimator.

The TCO Calculator compares the total cost of running workloads on-premises versus migrating them to Azure. It is a migration-decision tool, not a service-level pricing estimator for a new deployment.
